items.stem: Which type of radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper?
items.answer: Alpha
items.markingKey: α: stopped by paper/few cm of air; β: by a few mm of aluminium; γ: reduced by thick lead/concrete.

items.stem: Explain why alpha radiation is the most dangerous inside the body but the least dangerous outside it.
items.answer: Alpha is highly ionising, so inside it damages nearby cells strongly; outside it is stopped by the dead outer layer of skin or a few cm of air.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem: Explain how alpha, beta and gamma radiation are deflected differently in an electric field.
items.answer: α (positive) deflects towards the negative plate, β (negative) deflects more strongly towards the positive plate as it is much lighter, γ is undeflected (no charge).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for α, β, γ.

items.stem: A student measures count rates (counts/min) from a source: no absorber 720; paper 720; 3 mm aluminium 19; 2 cm lead 16. Background is 15 counts/min. Deduce which types of radiation the source emits, explaining each step.
items.answer: No alpha (paper hardly changes the count). Aluminium greatly reduces the count, so beta is present. Count after aluminium is about background, so no gamma.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for reasoning on alpha, beta and gamma using the absorber data and background.

items.stem: A student measures count rates (counts/min) from a source: no absorber 850; paper 850; 3 mm aluminium 26; 2 cm lead 23. Background is 20 counts/min. Deduce which types of radiation the source emits, explaining each step.
items.answer: No alpha (paper hardly changes the count). Aluminium greatly reduces the count, so beta is present. Count after aluminium is about background, so no gamma.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for reasoning on alpha, beta and gamma using the absorber data and background.

items.stem: A Geiger–Müller tube placed near a technetium tracer records a corrected count rate of 800 counts/min. The background count rate is 25 counts/min and the half-life is 3 days. (a) Describe how to measure the background count rate. (b) Estimate the time for the corrected count rate to fall below 45.0 counts/min.
items.answer: (a) Remove all sources, record counts over several minutes and find the mean per minute. (b) Just over 12 days (4 half-lives)

items.stem: Which type of radiation is the most ionising?
items.answer: Alpha
items.markingKey: α particles are large and highly charged so they ionise strongly.

items.stem: Explain why the count rate measured near a source should be corrected for background radiation.
items.answer: Background radiation is always present and adds to the counts; it must be measured without the source and subtracted to get the count rate from the source alone.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem: A Geiger–Müller tube placed near a sodium tracer records a corrected count rate of 960 counts/min. The background count rate is 25 counts/min and the half-life is 4 hours. (a) Explain why the count rate fluctuates even though the half-life is constant. (b) State two sources of background radiation.
items.answer: (a) Radioactive decay is random; the number decaying each second varies. (b) Radon gas from rocks; cosmic rays (or food, buildings, medical).

items.stem: A beta particle is
options: a fast-moving electron emitted from the nucleus
items.answer: a fast-moving electron emitted from the nucleus
items.markingKey: β⁻ forms when a neutron changes into a proton and an electron.

items.stem: Explain why gamma radiation passes through most materials while alpha does not.
items.answer: Gamma has no charge and no mass, so it interacts weakly; alpha is large and highly charged and loses energy quickly by ionising.

items.stem: Explain why a Geiger counter detects alpha particles only if it is very close to the source.
items.answer: Alpha particles travel only a few cm in air before losing their energy.

items.stem: A student measures count rates (counts/min) from a source: no absorber 600; paper 600; 3 mm aluminium 360; 2 cm lead 180. Background is 30 counts/min. Deduce which types of radiation the source emits, explaining each step.
items.answer: No alpha (paper hardly changes the count). Aluminium greatly reduces the count, so beta is present. Count after aluminium stays above background, so gamma is present.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for reasoning on alpha, beta and gamma using the absorber data and background.

items.stem: A student measures count rates (counts/min) from a source: no absorber 720; paper 715; 3 mm aluminium 17; 2 cm lead 216. Background is 15 counts/min. Deduce which types of radiation the source emits, explaining each step.
items.answer: No alpha (paper hardly changes the count). Aluminium greatly reduces the count, so beta is present. Count after aluminium is about background, so no gamma.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for reasoning on alpha, beta and gamma using the absorber data and background.

items.stem: A student measures count rates (counts/min) from a source: no absorber 850; paper 850; 3 mm aluminium 17; 2 cm lead 255. Background is 15 counts/min. Deduce which types of radiation the source emits, explaining each step.
items.answer: No alpha (paper hardly changes the count). Aluminium greatly reduces the count, so beta is present. Count after aluminium is about background, so no gamma.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for reasoning on alpha, beta and gamma using the absorber data and background.

items.stem: A smoke detector contains a small americium-241 source that emits alpha particles. (a) State which type of radiation is suitable and explain why. (b) Explain the difference between irradiation and contamination in this context.
items.answer: (a) Depends on penetration: alpha for short-range ionisation, beta for thin sheet thickness, gamma to pass through the body or packaging. (b) Irradiation: exposed to radiation from outside, does not become radioactive; contamination: radioactive material gets on/in the object.

items.stem: A Geiger–Müller tube placed near a protactinium source records a corrected count rate of 960 counts/min. The background count rate is 25 counts/min and the half-life is 6 minutes. (a) Calculate the corrected count rate after 18 minutes. (b) Explain why the count rate fluctuates even though the half-life is constant. (c) Describe how to measure the background count rate.
items.answer: (a) 120 counts/min (b) Radioactive decay is random; the number decaying each second varies. (c) Remove all sources, record counts over several minutes and find the mean per minute.

items.stem: Which of these is a source of background radiation?
items.answer: Radon gas from rocks
items.markingKey: Background: radon, rocks/buildings, cosmic rays, food and drink, medical sources.

items.stem: Explain why radon gas is a significant source of background radiation in some homes.
items.answer: Radon from granite rock seeps into buildings; it is breathed in and emits alpha particles inside the lungs.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why radon gas is a significant source of background radiation in some homes. (b) Explain why gamma radiation passes through most materials while alpha does not.
items.answer: (a) Radon from granite rock seeps into buildings; it is breathed in and emits alpha particles inside the lungs. (b) Gamma has no charge and no mass, so it interacts weakly; alpha is large and highly charged and loses energy quickly by ionising.

items.stem: A student measures count rates (counts/min) from a source: no absorber 850; paper 850; 3 mm aluminium 28; 2 cm lead 25. Background is 24 counts/min. Deduce which types of radiation the source emits, explaining each step.
items.answer: No alpha (paper hardly changes the count). Aluminium greatly reduces the count, so beta is present. Count after aluminium is about background, so no gamma.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for reasoning on alpha, beta and gamma using the absorber data and background.

items.stem: A Geiger–Müller tube placed near an iodine source records a corrected count rate of 1600 counts/min. The background count rate is 30 counts/min and the half-life is 5 minutes. (a) Calculate the corrected count rate after 10 minutes. (b) Estimate the time for the corrected count rate to fall below 90.0 counts/min.
items.answer: (a) 400 counts/min (b) Just over 20 minutes (4 half-lives)

items.stem: Radioactive decay is described as random. This means
options: it is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay
decay can be speeded up by heating
all nuclei decay at the same time
items.answer: it is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay
items.markingKey: Each nucleus has a fixed probability of decay per second; the moment is unpredictable.

items.stem: Explain why the nucleon number does not change in beta decay.
items.answer: A neutron changes into a proton (and electron): the total number of nucleons stays the same.

items.stem: Explain why a nucleus may emit gamma radiation after alpha or beta decay.
items.answer: The new nucleus is left with excess energy, which it releases as a gamma ray.

items.stem: Ra-226 (proton number 88) decays by alpha emission to form Rn. Write the decay equation and give the nucleon and proton numbers of Rn.
items.answer: Rn: nucleon number 222, proton number 86. Ra-226 (Z = 88) → Rn-222 (Z = 86) + α (He-4, Z = 2)
items.markingKey: 1 mark nucleon number 222; 1 mark proton number 86; 1 mark balanced equation (top and bottom numbers conserved).

items.stem: I-131 (proton number 53) decays by beta emission to form Xe. Write the decay equation and give the nucleon and proton numbers of Xe.
items.answer: Xe: nucleon number 131, proton number 54. I-131 (Z = 53) → Xe-131 (Z = 54) + β (e, Z = −1)
items.markingKey: 1 mark nucleon number 131; 1 mark proton number 54; 1 mark balanced equation (top and bottom numbers conserved).

items.stem: U-238 (proton number 92) decays by alpha emission to form Th. Write the decay equation and give the nucleon and proton numbers of Th.
items.answer: Th: nucleon number 234, proton number 90. U-238 (Z = 92) → Th-234 (Z = 90) + α (He-4, Z = 2)
items.markingKey: 1 mark nucleon number 234; 1 mark proton number 90; 1 mark balanced equation (top and bottom numbers conserved).

items.stem: A Geiger–Müller tube placed near a sodium tracer records a corrected count rate of 960 counts/min. The background count rate is 20 counts/min and the half-life is 6 days. (a) Calculate the corrected count rate after 18 days. (b) Estimate the time for the corrected count rate to fall below 54.0 counts/min.
items.answer: (a) 120 counts/min (b) Just over 24 days (4 half-lives)

items.stem: Uranium-238 (Z = 92) decays by the sequence alpha, then beta, then beta. Find the nucleon number and proton number of the final nucleus, showing each step.
items.answer: Nucleon number 234, proton number 92
items.markingKey: α: A − 4, Z − 2; β: A unchanged, Z + 1. 1 mark per correct step, 1 mark final answer.

items.stem: Explain why radioactive decay is described as spontaneous.
items.answer: It is not affected by external conditions such as temperature, pressure or chemical reactions.

items.stem: Explain why a sample with a large number of nuclei gives a fairly predictable count rate even though decay is random.
items.answer: With many nuclei, random variations average out; the fraction decaying per second is constant.

items.stem: Co-60 (proton number 27) decays by beta emission to form Ni. Write the decay equation and give the nucleon and proton numbers of Ni.
items.answer: Ni: nucleon number 60, proton number 28. Co-60 (Z = 27) → Ni-60 (Z = 28) + β (e, Z = −1)
items.markingKey: 1 mark nucleon number 60; 1 mark proton number 28; 1 mark balanced equation (top and bottom numbers conserved).

items.stem: Po-210 (proton number 84) decays by alpha emission to form Pb. Write the decay equation and give the nucleon and proton numbers of Pb.
items.answer: Pb: nucleon number 206, proton number 82. Po-210 (Z = 84) → Pb-206 (Z = 82) + α (He-4, Z = 2)
items.markingKey: 1 mark nucleon number 206; 1 mark proton number 82; 1 mark balanced equation (top and bottom numbers conserved).

items.stem: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is
options: the time for the mass of the sample to halve exactly
the time taken for half the nuclei in a sample to decay
half the time for all the nuclei to decay
the time for one nucleus to decay
items.answer: the time taken for half the nuclei in a sample to decay
items.markingKey: Half-life = time for activity (or number of undecayed nuclei) to halve.

items.stem: Explain what half-life and type of radiation would be best for a thickness gauge for paper production.
items.answer: Half-life long (years); beta radiation, because the count must not fall noticeably during use; beta is partly absorbed by paper so changes in thickness change the count.
items.markingKey: 1 mark half-life; 1 mark radiation type; 1 mark reason.

items.stem: A tracer is used in a hospital. The number of half-lives that pass is tripled. Explain how the activity after the same time changes.
items.answer: The activity after the same time triples.
items.markingKey: Using activity halves each half-life: activity after the same time ∝ number of half-lives that pass; factor = 3.00 = 3.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A sample has an activity of 3200 Bq. Its half-life is 6 days. Calculate its activity after 30 days.
items.answer: 100 Bq
items.markingKey: 30 days = 5 half-lives; 3200 ÷ 2^5 = 100 Bq.

items.stem: The activity of a source falls from 6400 Bq to 400 Bq in 120 hours. Calculate its half-life.
items.answer: 30 hours
items.markingKey: 6400 → 400 is 4 halvings; half-life = 120/4 = 30 hours.

items.stem: The activity of a source falls from 960 Bq to 60.0 Bq in 48 years. Calculate its half-life.
items.answer: 12 years
items.markingKey: 960 → 60.0 is 4 halvings; half-life = 48/4 = 12 years.

items.stem: A Geiger counter records 1300 counts/min near a source. The background count is 20 counts/min. The half-life is 2 minutes. Calculate the count rate the counter will record after 6 minutes.
items.answer: 180 counts/min
items.markingKey: Corrected rate = 1300 − 20 = 1280; 6 min = 3 half-lives → 1280/8 = 160; add background back: 180 counts/min. Not subtracting background is the usual error.

items.stem: A Geiger counter records 1320 counts/min near a source. The background count is 40 counts/min. The half-life is 5 minutes. Calculate the count rate the counter will record after 15 minutes.
items.answer: 200 counts/min
items.markingKey: Corrected rate = 1320 − 40 = 1280; 15 min = 3 half-lives → 1280/8 = 160; add background back: 200 counts/min. Not subtracting background is the usual error.

items.stem: Explain what half-life and type of radiation would be best for a medical tracer injected into a patient.
items.answer: Half-life short (hours); gamma radiation, because it must be detected outside the body and should not stay active in the body for long.
items.markingKey: 1 mark half-life; 1 mark radiation type; 1 mark reason.

items.stem: A sample has an activity of 2400 Bq. Its half-life is 6 days. Calculate its activity after 24 days.
items.answer: 150 Bq
items.markingKey: 24 days = 4 half-lives; 2400 ÷ 2^4 = 150 Bq.

items.stem: A Geiger–Müller tube placed near a sodium tracer records a corrected count rate of 800 counts/min. The background count rate is 20 counts/min and the half-life is 2 hours. (a) Calculate the reading the counter shows after 6 hours. (b) Estimate the time for the corrected count rate to fall below 45.0 counts/min.
items.answer: (a) 120 counts/min (b) Just over 8 hours (4 half-lives)
items.markingKey: (a) add background [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: A sample has an activity of 960 Bq. Its half-life is 8 years. Calculate its activity after 32 years.
items.markingKey: 32 years = 4 half-lives; 960 ÷ 2^4 = 60.0 Bq.

items.stem: Which is a correct safety precaution when handling radioactive sources in school?
options: Use tongs and keep the source pointed away from people
Keep the source in your pocket
Hold the source in your hand briefly
items.answer: Use tongs and keep the source pointed away from people
items.markingKey: Increase distance, reduce time, use shielding; never handle with bare hands.

items.stem: Explain the difference between irradiation and contamination.
items.answer: Irradiation is exposure to radiation from an external source (you do not become radioactive); contamination is when radioactive material gets onto or into the body or object, so it keeps emitting radiation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem: Explain why ionising radiation can cause cancer.
items.answer: It ionises atoms in cells, damaging DNA; mutated cells can divide uncontrollably.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem: Explain what half-life and type of radiation would be best for tracing leaks in an underground water pipe.
items.answer: Half-life short (days); gamma radiation, because gamma passes through soil to the detector; short half-life so the water is not contaminated for long.
items.markingKey: 1 mark half-life; 1 mark radiation type; 1 mark reason.

items.stem: An archaeologist uses carbon-14 to date a wooden bowl. (a) Explain why the half-life of the source matters for this use. (b) Describe two safety precautions for workers.
items.answer: (a) Long half-life for steady count over years; short half-life for medical use so the dose to the patient is low. (b) Shielding (lead), handling with tongs/remote, minimise time, maximise distance, wear dosimeter badge (any two).

items.stem: A town council is deciding whether to allow food irradiation (gamma rays) at a local factory. Evaluate the benefits and risks.
items.answer: Benefits: kills microorganisms/gives clear diagnosis; the item does not become radioactive (irradiation not contamination); short or controlled exposure. Risks: workers/patients receive dose; source must be shielded and handled remotely; long-term storage of sources. Conclusion with justification.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each: benefit; irradiation vs contamination; risk to people; precaution (shielding/distance/time/half-life choice); justified conclusion (max 5).

items.stem: Why are radioactive sources stored in lead-lined boxes?

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a nucleus may emit gamma radiation after alpha or beta decay. (b) Explain why radioactive decay is described as spontaneous.
items.answer: (a) The new nucleus is left with excess energy, which it releases as a gamma ray. (b) It is not affected by external conditions such as temperature, pressure or chemical reactions.

items.stem: C-14 (proton number 6) decays by beta emission to form N. Write the decay equation and give the nucleon and proton numbers of N.
items.answer: N: nucleon number 14, proton number 7. C-14 (Z = 6) → N-14 (Z = 7) + β (e, Z = −1)
items.markingKey: 1 mark nucleon number 14; 1 mark proton number 7; 1 mark balanced equation (top and bottom numbers conserved).

items.stem: A Geiger–Müller tube placed near a technetium tracer records a corrected count rate of 3200 counts/min. The background count rate is 25 counts/min and the half-life is 6 minutes. (a) State two sources of background radiation. (b) Estimate the time for the corrected count rate to fall below 180 counts/min.
items.answer: (a) Radon gas from rocks; cosmic rays (or food, buildings, medical). (b) Just over 24 minutes (4 half-lives)

items.stem: A Geiger–Müller tube placed near a protactinium source records a corrected count rate of 2400 counts/min. The background count rate is 20 counts/min and the half-life is 2 hours. (a) Calculate the corrected count rate after 6 hours. (b) Describe how to measure the background count rate. (c) State two sources of background radiation.
items.answer: (a) 300 counts/min (b) Remove all sources, record counts over several minutes and find the mean per minute. (c) Radon gas from rocks; cosmic rays (or food, buildings, medical).

items.stem: A tracer is used in a hospital. The number of half-lives that pass is halved. State and explain how the activity after the same time changes.
items.answer: The activity after the same time halves.
items.markingKey: Using activity halves each half-life: activity after the same time ∝ number of half-lives that pass; factor = 0.500 = 0.500. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A tracer is used in a hospital. The number of half-lives that pass is increased by 50%. Explain how the activity after the same time changes.
items.answer: The activity after the same time increases by 50%.
items.markingKey: Using activity halves each half-life: activity after the same time ∝ number of half-lives that pass; factor = 1.50 = 1.50. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A sample has an activity of 800 Bq. Its half-life is 4 hours. Calculate its activity after 8 hours.
items.answer: 200 Bq
items.markingKey: 8 hours = 2 half-lives; 800 ÷ 2^2 = 200 Bq.

items.stem: A Geiger counter records 830 counts/min near a source. The background count is 30 counts/min. The half-life is 2 minutes. Calculate the count rate the counter will record after 6 minutes.
items.answer: 130 counts/min
items.markingKey: Corrected rate = 830 − 30 = 800; 6 min = 3 half-lives → 800/8 = 100; add background back: 130 counts/min. Not subtracting background is the usual error.

items.stem: A tracer is used in a hospital. The number of half-lives that pass is multiplied by 4. State and explain how the activity after the same time changes.
items.answer: The activity after the same time becomes 4 times bigger.
items.markingKey: Using activity halves each half-life: activity after the same time ∝ number of half-lives that pass; factor = 4.00 = 4.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A factory uses a radioactive source and detector to monitor the thickness of aluminium foil. Explain why ionising radiation can be harmful to living cells.
items.answer: It ionises molecules, damaging DNA and causing mutation or cell death.

items.stem: Food is passed through a beam of gamma radiation before packaging. (a) State which type of radiation is suitable and explain why. (b) Explain why the half-life of the source matters for this use.
items.answer: (a) Depends on penetration: alpha for short-range ionisation, beta for thin sheet thickness, gamma to pass through the body or packaging. (b) Long half-life for steady count over years; short half-life for medical use so the dose to the patient is low.
